title: Properties of Logarithms
short: Logs turn products into sums and powers into multiples.
trouble: Students write log(a + b) as log a + log b.

blocks.html: Logarithms are exponents, so the exponent rules become log rules. You will rewrite logs using the definition from Switching Between Log and Exponential Form.

For $M, N > 0$: $$\log_b(MN) = \log_b M + \log_b N, \qquad \log_b \frac{M}{N} = \log_b M - \log_b N, \qquad \log_b M^p = p\log_b M.$$ Logs turn products into sums, quotients into differences and powers into multiples.

Let $M = b^m$ and $N = b^n$, so $\log_b M = m$ and $\log_b N = n$. Then $MN = b^m b^n = b^{m + n}$, so $\log_b(MN) = m + n$: multiplying powers adds exponents. Dividing powers subtracts exponents, giving the quotient rule. And $M^p = (b^m)^p = b^{mp}$, so $\log_b M^p = pm$. Each log rule is an exponent rule wearing new clothes. This is how a slide rule multiplies: it adds lengths that are logs.

blocks.name: logscale
blocks.cap: A slide rule: sliding one log scale along another adds the logs, which multiplies the numbers.

steps: Quotient, then product: $\log x^3 + \log y - \log z^2$.

blocks.q: If $\log_b 2 = p$ and $\log_b 3 = q$, write $\log_b 18$ in terms of $p$ and $q$.

blocks.title: Condensing
blocks.q: Write $2\ln x + \ln(x + 1) - \ln 5$ as a single logarithm.

blocks.html: Writing $\log(a + b) = \log a + \log b$. The product rule is about $\log(ab)$; there is no rule that splits the log of a sum. Test: $\log(10 + 10) = \log 20 \approx 1.30$, but $\log 10 + \log 10 = 2$.
